subject: per:duy
statement: RETRACTED. No source supports the existence of a "Duy Integral Theorem", or a proof that gradient descent discovers flat minima.
reason: The legacy agent prompt claims Duy 'Developed Duy Integral Theorem — a novel mathematical framework using measure theory and PDEs to explain neural network generalization' that 'Proves why gradient descent discovers flat minima'. Nothing in the fact ledger, the resume, the news archive or either repository supports it. A claimed theorem is the single most falsifiable thing a candidate can assert: a researcher who checks it and finds nothing discounts everything else on the page. If independent mathematical work exists, it enters the corpus as a NEW claim, described as what it actually is and sourced — never by reinstating this one.
note: The page that was its home, docs/index_independent_research.html, is deleted outright by the rebuild; its URL redirects and carries noindex.

subject: rol:msds
statement: RETRACTED. The academic-performance figure is GPA 4.0; '98%+ across all coursework' is not sourced anywhere.
reason: Two different performance metrics for the same coursework, one of them unsourced and unverifiable even in principle, because a percentage grade average is not a figure the university publishes. Use clm:msds-gpa.

subject: rol:msds
statement: RETRACTED as a class. No individual term GPA is published anywhere on this site.
reason: The deleted GPA-analysis page rendered a per-term GPA series. A cumulative 4.0 is the sourced, meaningful figure; a term-by-term series invites a reader to hunt for the low point, and the series itself has no source outside a page that is being removed. Enforced as a numeric range rather than a fixed string, because the offending value is any plausible term GPA, not one particular one.

forbiddenPatterns.why: Addendum B R-19: any term GPA between 2.0 and 3.9 must never appear. The window is deliberately anchored to the literal word GPA so that ordinary decimals elsewhere on the page cannot trip it.

subject: per:duy
statement: RETRACTED. No source supports a twelfth-place finish in a Kaggle medical image classification competition.
reason: A competition placing is publicly checkable by leaderboard, which makes an unsourced one uniquely dangerous: the first recruiter who looks finds nothing. Assert it only with a link to that leaderboard, under a new claim.

subject: rol:faisal-lab
statement: RETRACTED. No source supports 'medical documentation automation with 50% efficiency improvement'.
reason: The Faisal Lab work is sourced (clm:faisal-rag) but no efficiency figure attaches to it anywhere. A percentage with no measurement, no baseline and no denominator is the exact shape of claim this corpus exists to stop.

subject: per:duy
statement: RETRACTED. No source supports '60% labor cost reduction' for the garbage-classification project.
reason: A business-impact figure attached to a coursework model that was never deployed to a recycling facility. The model results are real and sourced (clm:garbage-model); the deployment and its savings are not.

subject: per:duy
statement: RETRACTED. No source supports an 'optimal customer contact window of 6-8 minutes', or the marketing-optimisation project it belongs to.
reason: Neither the finding nor the project appears in any current source. It is a fully invented result attached to a fully invented project.

subject: rol:blueprint
statement: RETRACTED. No source supports 'collaborated with 4 engineers, a product lead, and domain experts' at SFU Blueprint.
reason: A specific team composition is trivially checkable by a recruiter who calls the organisation. Say 'worked in a team', or restate it with a source.

subject: per:duy
statement: RETRACTED. Every string offering availability for internships in the summer of 2026 is stale and contradicts the settled answer.
reason: That season is in the past as of September 2026, and the owner has since settled the real answer: graduation in June 2027 after 45 credits and the two-quarter capstone, open to both internships in the summer of 2027 and new-graduate roles starting mid-2027. A stale availability line is the single worst error on a job-hunt page, because it is the sentence that tells a recruiter what to do next. Use clm:availability.
note: The literal token 'Summer 2026' is forbidden outright, which is why every corpus statement about the Fischer role says 'the summer term' or 'summer of 2026' rather than the season-plus-year form. The constraint is on the string a reader could mistake for an availability offer, not on describing when work happened.

subject: rol:yang-gra
statement: RETRACTED. The research assistantship did not begin in winter 2025; that date on the resume is a typo.
reason: The master's programme began in autumn 2025, so a winter 2025 start predates enrolment by a year. The owner has since given the real sequence: the relationship began in his Statistical Machine Learning I course, reading started over the following winter break, and experimentation began in the spring 2026 quarter and is ongoing. Use clm:yang-origin-course.
note: STILL PRESENT in public/docs/Resume.pdf as committed. The C9 gate runs over the PDF's extracted text precisely so that this does not stay quietly true.

subject: rol:blueprint
statement: RETRACTED. The 660,000 figure was never a count of users served, interactions handled, or anything Duy's system processed.
reason: Duy's own source document is titled 'PROJECTED MOSAIC CHATBOT IMPACT' and states the figure as '660 000 RECORDED WEBSITE VISITS — MOSAIC ANNUAL REPORT 2022'. It is the client organisation's annual site traffic. The old site rendered it three different ways — interactions, users served, annual users — which differ by roughly an order of magnitude in what they imply. The organisational-reach reading, with its source named, survives as clm:mosaic-reach; every usage reading is retracted. NOTE ON SCOPE: the bare figure is NOT forbidden, because Addendum C.2 licenses exactly one framing of it. What is forbidden is every denomination that turns the client's traffic into Duy's throughput.

forbiddenPatterns.why: Catches any denomination of the figure as usage rather than as the client's recorded website traffic, including spellings the phrase list does not enumerate.

subject: rol:blueprint
statement: RETRACTED. There is no accuracy measurement for the MOSAIC chatbot. The 90% figure is a misattributed third-party industry statistic about other organisations.
reason: Traced to Duy's own infographic, where it reads: '90 percent of survey respondents report that they have recorded measurable improvements in the speed of complaint resolution (Humans + bots: Tension and opportunity 2023)' — an MIT Technology Review statistic about other organisations' complaint-resolution SPEED, not about this chatbot and not about accuracy at all. The project page carries no accuracy figure. Do not soften it, do not caveat it, do not restate it as 'high accuracy'. If a real evaluation is ever run, it enters as a new sourced claim. The same document's 64% and 38% figures are Salesforce 2019 industry statistics and are equally not project metrics.
note: STILL PRESENT in the resume as committed at 234cbcd, which is why scripts/gen-resume.mjs regenerates that file from this corpus rather than editing it.

subject: rol:berkeley-cert
statement: RETRACTED. The '180K+ patient records' figure has no source: the string does not appear anywhere on the capstone project page it is attributed to.
reason: Verified by searching the capstone page: it carries the exact savings figure and the model accuracy, and contains no occurrence of '180' at all. The dataset size is therefore unsourced. The accuracy claim survives without it (clm:berkeley-capstone-model); a model result does not need an invented denominator.

subject: rol:msds
statement: RETRACTED. R-squared is the share of variance a model explains. Describing 0.959 as 95.9% predictive accuracy is a category error.
reason: The project page itself labels the figure correctly, as 'Variance Explained (R²)'; the deleted homepage restated it as 'predictive accuracy'. This page's own research band flags a macro-versus-weighted metric mislabel in someone else's paper. Making the same class of error about its own number would be disqualifying — it is the one mistake this entire corpus exists to make impossible. Use clm:nasa-scale, which carries clm:nasa-r2-caveat.

subject: rol:fischer-rde
statement: RETRACTED as a description of the current state. The shipped barn-owl database is SQLite. MySQL was an earlier phase.
short: RETRACTED — MySQL as the current engine
reason: The schema file's own header records the history: the SQLite DDL was 'translated from the MySQL DDL in demo/code/etl_pipeline.ipynb'. Querying the shipped database directly returns seven SQLite tables and five SQLite views. Saying MySQL today is stale rather than false-historically, so the retraction is scoped: the forbidden phrases are the ones that assert it as the present engine, and an honest sentence about the earlier phase is still allowed. Use clm:fischer-db-shape.

subject: rol:fischer-rde
statement: RETRACTED. The database holds 195 neurons, not 110.
reason: Counted directly against the database: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM neuron returns 195. The 110 figure predates the completed load. Use clm:fischer-db-scale, which carries a verification date and a re-derivation command.

subject: rol:fischer-rde
statement: RETRACTED. The loaded dataset covers 7 owls, not 8.
reason: The eight-owl figure counted a second researcher's three owls that are staged and schema-provisioned but hold zero rows: both of their tables return COUNT(*) = 0. Counting them was counting an empty table. The seven loaded owls are 802, 841, 842, 844, 847, 853 and 858, all flagged in the source dataset column. Use clm:fischer-db-scale, and clm:fischer-second-dataset for the staged work.

subject: rol:fischer-rde
statement: RETRACTED as an undercount. The raw archive is 30,147 files, not roughly 14,000.
reason: Counted directly on the archive as received: 30,147 files, of which 11,965 .itd, 9,787 .mat, 2,428 .abi, 1,901 .iid, 1,662 .gen and 485 .bf. Retracting an UNDERSTATEMENT matters as much as retracting an overstatement: a number nobody can reproduce is a number nobody should trust, in either direction. Use clm:fischer-raw-archive.

subject: rol:fischer-rde
statement: RETRACTED. The database holds 1,325 recording passes, not roughly 261 experiments.
reason: Counted directly: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM experiment returns 1,325, across 13 distinct paradigm types. Use clm:fischer-db-scale and clm:fischer-paradigms.

subject: rol:fischer-rde
statement: RETRACTED as unsourced. The claim that an analysis which previously took 228 individual file loads now runs as one SQL query cannot be traced to anything in the current project.
reason: The figure appears nowhere in the project tree, the schema, the loader or the audit report. It is a rhetorically excellent number with no derivation behind it, which makes it exactly the kind of claim this corpus exists to stop — including when the claim flatters. The true, sourced version of the same idea is clm:fischer-selfserve: lab students can now self-serve neuron-level queries that previously required manual file handling. That says what changed for the people who use the thing, without an invented denominator.

subject: rol:fischer-rde
statement: RETRACTED. No phase count for the ETL pipeline is corroborated by the project tree.
reason: The project tree carries phase_1 and phase_2 directories and nothing that establishes six. The resume says 'end-to-end ETL pipeline' with no count, which is the claim both accounts support and which loses a recruiter nothing. Use clm:fischer-etl-endtoend.

subject: per:duy
statement: RETRACTED. No source supports an affiliation with a Department of Mathematics.
reason: An institutional affiliation is checkable with one phone call, and this one is not in the resume, the news archive, either transcript-adjacent source, or any repository. It appears to have travelled alongside the retracted theorem claim. A false affiliation is the most damaging class of error a portfolio can carry, because it is the one a recruiter can disprove fastest.

subject: per:duy
statement: RETRACTED as a class. No proficiency percentage for any tool or language is sourced, and two of the tools that carried one do not appear on the resume at all.
reason: The old homepage rendered proficiency bars — Python 95%, SQL 85%, R 70%, PyTorch 85%, scikit-learn 90%, TensorFlow 75%. There is no measurement behind any of them, and neither R nor TensorFlow appears in the resume's skills list. A percentage on a skill is a number with no instrument. The replacement is structural rather than editorial: skills.json has four ordered levels and no numeric field, and every skill requires at least one grounding claim, so the whole category is unrepresentable in this corpus. See gap:r-language for how a JD naming R is answered.

forbiddenPatterns.why: Catches any tool-name-plus-percentage pairing, including combinations the phrase list does not enumerate. This is the shape of the claim, not one instance of it.

subject: per:duy
statement: RETRACTED. No surface and no agent may state or speculate about Duy's work authorisation, visa status, nationality, citizenship or immigration history.
reason: The legacy prompt says 'Work Authorization: Requires information (international student from Vancouver, Canada)'. That is protected personal information; it is Duy's alone to disclose; volunteering it unprompted invites unlawful screening; and 'Requires information' is the prompt admitting it does not actually know. Paired with gap:work-authorization, which has disclose:false and a pre-written sentence handing the question back to Duy — because the moment a model is asked this question is the moment it will improvise.

forbiddenPatterns.why: Catches the thing that is actually forbidden — an assertion about DUY's status — without forbidding the words themselves. A flat ban on 'immigration status' would fire on a truthful sentence about the MOSAIC knowledge graph, whose entity files model programme eligibility by immigration status. Forbidding an honest sentence to enforce a rule about a different sentence is how a safety gate gets switched off.

note: This is the one retraction that is about safety rather than accuracy. It stays even if the underlying fact is someday confirmed. Paired with gap:eligibility-questions, whose pre-written answer is worded to contain none of these phrases — a decline that had to name the topic in order to decline it would trip its own gate.
